strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: enabling low-variance pathwise (deterministic) policy gradients in a fully on-policy setting, avoiding the memory and stability issues of replay-buffer-based off-policy methods.

Very thorough empirical evaluation spanning 30+ tasks across two distinct GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (DMC locomotion and ManiSkill manipulation), with appropriately tuned baselines (PPO, SAC, FastTD3) and multiple seeds.

Careful ablation study isolating the contribution of each architectural/algorithmic component (HL-Gauss cross-entropy loss, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary loss, KL regularization) at two different batch sizes, providing useful practical guidance.
Novel 'reliable performance' metric offers an interesting and practically relevant lens on training stability beyond simple mean return curves.
Demonstrates substantial memory savings versus off-policy alternatives (FastTD3) while matching or exceeding their performance, and shows competitive wall-clock efficiency versus PPO.
The toy illustrative experiment (Section 2.3) nicely builds intuition for why surrogate quality matters for pathwise gradients.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (e.g., inconsistent benefit of auxiliary loss, cases where PPO outperforms REPPO, framework-dependent wall-clock results), and provides code in two frameworks for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is largely a careful combination of existing ideas (TD(λ) targets, maximum-entropy RL, REPS-style KL trust regions, HL-Gauss/C51, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary losses) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the core theoretical question of why on-policy data can yield accurate-enough Q-functions for pathwise gradients is not rigorously analyzed, only empirically observed.

No formal bias/variance analysis or convergence argument for the biased pathwise gradient under on-policy Q-learning; claims about REPPO 'unlocking' on-policy pathwise gradients rest entirely on empirical results without theoretical grounding.

Missing empirical comparisons to closely related KL/entropy-based methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., MPO, V-MPO, PQN), which would better contextualize REPPO's contribution relative to prior KL-regularized or hybrid on/off-policy approaches.

The claim of strong hyperparameter robustness across 30+ tasks with a single hyperparameter set is asserted but not directly validated through a hyperparameter sensitivity study; robustness is inferred rather than demonstrated.
Uneven number of seeds across methods (10 for REPPO vs. 4 for PPO baselines, 5 for FastTD3) could introduce some asymmetry in confidence interval comparisons.

Presentation issues: broken cross-reference ('??' for implementation details appendix), dense/hard-to-parse aggregate figures with many overlapping baseline variants, and the toy example in Sec 2.3 is fairly informal/anecdotal.
Auxiliary task and normalization contributions are described as inconsistent or environment-dependent, weakening the generality of some proposed architectural components.
Wall-clock comparisons are only conducted in JAX (with torch admitted to be worse due to implementation issues), limiting the strength of the efficiency claims across frameworks.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated research question: whether pathwise (DPG-style) policy gradients can be made reliable using only on-policy data, avoiding the memory and off-policy stability issues of replay-buffer-based methods.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning over 30 tasks across two GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (MuJoCo Playground DMC and ManiSkill3), covering locomotion and manipulation.

Useful and practically relevant ablation study isolating the contribution of individual components (HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction loss, KL regularization) at two different batch/data scales.
Memory-footprint comparison against FastTD3 under matched buffer budgets is a valuable and underexplored axis of comparison that highlights a genuine practical advantage of the proposed method.
The illustrative toy experiment (6-hump camel function) nicely conveys the qualitative bias/variance trade-off between score-function and pathwise gradients with surrogate models of varying quality.
Reasonable discussion of related work situating REPPO relative to MPO/V-MPO, PQN, and off-policy MPS algorithms (FastTD3, Parallel Q-Learning).
Authors commit to releasing code in both JAX and PyTorch, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: the method largely recombines existing components (REPS/TRPO-style KL constraints, SAC-style maximum-entropy objective, TD(λ) targets, HL-Gauss from Farebrother et al. 2024, layer normalization, and self-predictive auxiliary losses from Schwarzer et al. 2021), without a clearly new theoretical or algorithmic idea beyond the integration itself.

There appears to be an error in the Lagrange multiplier update equations (18) and (19): both the entropy coefficient α and the KL coefficient β updates use the same term (H[πθ(x)] − Htarget), whereas Algorithm 1 correctly uses the KL divergence term for β. This inconsistency is not explained and raises concerns about the correctness/care taken in the technical presentation.

No theoretical analysis (e.g., bias bounds, convergence guarantees) is provided for using a biased, on-policy-only trained surrogate Q-function to drive pathwise policy gradients; the entire argument for why this works rests on empirical demonstration.

Statistical rigor of comparisons is limited in places: PPO baselines use only 4 seeds versus 10 for REPPO, and strong claims of 'statistically significant' improvement are made without clearly reported significance tests beyond bootstrapped CIs in aggregate plots.

Fairness of baseline tuning is unclear—while the authors state they retuned PPO for higher sample efficiency, it is not clear whether comparable tuning effort/budget was applied to REPPO's own hyperparameters versus baselines, especially regarding FastTD3 under the constrained buffer setting (unclear if FastTD3 hyperparameters were retuned for the smaller buffer or simply truncated).

The paper's wall-clock efficiency claims are undercut by its own appendix, which notes REPPO is competitive with PPO only under JAX and 'struggles somewhat in torch,' limiting the generality of the practical efficiency claims.

The automatic tuning of γ based on max environment steps and the heuristic min/max range selection for HL-Gauss are introduced without ablation or justification, despite being presented as part of the 'robust' default hyperparameter set.

Several individual-environment results show REPPO underperforming or converging to suboptimal solutions (e.g., FingerSpin, RollBall) with only brief post-hoc conjecture about exploration/premature convergence, rather than deeper analysis of failure modes.

Minor presentation issues: several typos/incomplete cross-references (e.g., '??' reference for implementation details, 'environemnts', 'forn'), and the manuscript's claims of broad hyperparameter robustness rely on a single fixed hyperparameter set rather than a systematic sensitivity sweep.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important question: whether pathwise (deterministic/reparameterized) policy gradients can be made stable with purely on-policy data, avoiding the memory and off-policy instability issues of large replay buffers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 30+ environments across two distinct GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (Mujoco Playground DMC and ManiSkill3), covering locomotion and manipulation with varying difficulty.

Strong methodological rigor in evaluation: multiple seeds (10 for REPPO), bootstrapped confidence intervals, and outlier-robust aggregate metrics (mean/median/IQM) following established best practices (Agarwal et al. 2021).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual architectural components (HL-Gauss cross-entropy loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction loss, KL regularization) at two different batch-size/data regimes, which clarifies which components matter and when.

Compelling practical results: REPPO achieves competitive or superior performance to PPO and even approaches/outperforms off-policy FastTD3 while using orders-of-magnitude smaller memory footprint, and shows good wall-clock efficiency.
The introduced 'reliable performance' metric is a useful and intuitive way to characterize policy stability during training, going beyond simple final-performance comparisons.
Good positioning relative to related work (PQN, MPO/V-MPO, FastTD3, TD3/SAC), clearly articulating what is reused versus novel.
Promise of both JAX and PyTorch implementations aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a careful combination of existing techniques (TD-λ targets, max-entropy RL, KL-constrained updates à la REPS/MPO, HL-Gauss classification loss, layer norm, self-predictive auxiliary tasks) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical insight; novelty is primarily in integration and engineering.

Theoretical justification for why on-policy critic training avoids the instability/bias issues that plague pathwise gradients in off-policy settings is thin; the argument is largely empirical/intuitive rather than formally analyzed (e.g., no bias-variance analysis of the biased pathwise gradient estimator in this specific on-policy regime).

The illustrative toy example (Section 2.3 / Appendix C.1) appears somewhat cherry-picked: the learning rate was explicitly chosen to favor the ground-truth pathwise gradient, and it is unclear how representative the 6-hump camel function and initialization near the optimum are of real RL dynamics.

There appears to be a typo/inconsistency in Equations 18-19 where both the entropy (α) and KL (β) multiplier updates reference the same entropy term (H[πθ(x)] − Htarget), which is likely an error but raises questions about the correctness of the reported update rule as presented.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat uneven: FastTD3 is only benchmarked on DMC locomotion tasks and not on ManiSkill, and it is unclear whether the tuned PPO baseline received comparably extensive hyperparameter search effort to REPPO, which could bias comparative conclusions.

For ManiSkill, the paper notes that mean-based confidence intervals are 'very broad,' with gains only clearly visible in median/IQM metrics, suggesting the improvement may not be robust/consistent across all seeds or tasks.
Some cross-references are broken (e.g., '??' for hyperparameter details in Section 4.1), suggesting incomplete polishing of the manuscript.

Despite motivating the work partly via language-model fine-tuning and robotics in the introduction, all experiments are confined to simulated locomotion/manipulation control; no validation on higher-dimensional observation spaces (e.g., images) or discrete/LLM settings is provided, which limits the generality of the claims made in the introduction.

The auxiliary loss and normalization components show inconsistent, environment-dependent effects (helpful in some tasks, harmful in others) without a clear predictive account of when they should be used, somewhat undercutting the paper's claim of broad hyperparameter robustness with 'a single hyperparameter set.'

strengths: Novel and interesting core idea: adapting pathwise (deterministic/reparameterized) policy gradients, traditionally used in off-policy algorithms like DDPG/SAC/TD3, to a fully on-policy setting without replay buffers, addressing a real practical bottleneck (memory footprint) in off-policy RL.

Very thorough empirical evaluation spanning 30+ tasks across two GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (Mujoco Playground DMC and ManiSkill3), with results reported using rigorous statistical aggregation (bootstrapped CIs, IQM, median) following best practices (Agarwal et al. 2021).

Comprehensive ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual architectural/algorithmic components (HL-Gauss cross-entropy loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-predictive loss, KL regularization) at multiple data-batch scales, clarifying which components matter most and when.

Strong practical results: REPPO is competitive with FastTD3 (an off-policy SOTA method) while using orders of magnitude less memory, and clearly outperforms PPO on sample efficiency, final performance, and training stability/reliability metrics.
Nice illustrative toy experiment (Section 2.2) that builds intuition for why pathwise gradients reduce variance relative to score-based estimators.
Extension to discrete action spaces (D-REPPO) and comparison against PQN, showing generality of the approach beyond continuous control.
Good engineering transparency: discussion of JAX vs PyTorch implementation trade-offs and honest acknowledgment of wall-clock measurement caveats (Appendix A).
Demonstrated hyperparameter robustness across many diverse tasks using a single hyperparameter configuration, which is valuable for practitioners.
Reasonably thorough related work section situating the method relative to trust-region methods, KL-regularized RL (MPO/VMPO), and hybrid on/off-policy approaches like PQN and FastTD3.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical grounding: the paper is largely empirically/heuristically motivated (e.g., why an on-policy-only trained Q-function yields sufficiently low-bias gradients, why the relaxed Lagrangian KL+entropy objective is stable) without formal analysis or convergence guarantees; the known discounting/occupancy issue (footnote 1) is acknowledged but not addressed.

Comparisons to some baselines (RPO, DPO) are dismissed briefly with a claim that the authors 'were unable to get performance above PPO... even with some hyperparameter tuning,' which is under-specified and raises concern about tuning effort/fairness of comparison.

Wall-clock efficiency claims are only substantiated in JAX; the PyTorch implementation reportedly underperforms due to framework-specific overheads, and FastTD3 (a key off-policy baseline) could not be run with a comparably fast implementation, weakening the wall-clock comparison's practical relevance since much real-world RL code is PyTorch-based.

Statistical rigor of the FastTD3 comparison is somewhat compromised by using only 5 seeds (vs 20 for REPPO/PPO) due to inability to replicate the claimed speed of FastTD3, which could affect the reliability of the reported confidence intervals for that particular comparison.

Auxiliary self-predictive loss is reported to have an 'inconsistent' (sometimes harmful) effect across environments without deeper analysis of what task properties predict when it helps vs hurts, limiting actionable guidance for practitioners.

The individual architectural components incorporated (HL-Gauss, layer norm, auxiliary tasks, KL/entropy Lagrangian tuning) are all adapted from prior work; the primary novelty is their combination and adaptation to the on-policy pathwise setting rather than fundamentally new techniques, somewhat limiting the conceptual novelty.

No direct empirical comparison to closely related KL-regularized methods (MPO, V-MPO) despite extensive discussion of their similarity in related work, leaving open how REPPO compares against these more directly analogous baselines.
In the discrete-action experiments, PQN slightly outperforms D-REPPO, and the explanation offered (lack of explicit exploration noise) is speculative and not verified via a targeted ablation.

Minor presentation issues, e.g., a broken/incomplete sentence regarding code availability, and a placeholder reference (??) for the HL-Gauss loss equation location, suggesting incomplete proofreading.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning >30 locomotion/manipulation tasks across two major GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (DMC via MuJoCo Playground, ManiSkill), plus an Atari-10 discrete variant, which is a non-trivial engineering and experimental effort.

The core idea of training Q-value surrogates purely from on-policy trajectories to enable pathwise (low-variance) policy gradients without large replay buffers is a reasonable and practically appealing direction, addressing a real memory/stability tension in RL.

Thorough ablation study (Subsection D.1) isolating the contribution of HL-Gauss cross-entropy loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction loss, and KL regularization at two data scales, which helps clarify which architectural choices matter most.

Practically useful evaluation axes beyond final return: wall-clock time, memory footprint, hyperparameter robustness across environments with a (mostly) fixed hyperparameter set, and a 'reliable success' stability metric that captures training degradation, not just asymptotic performance.

Reasonably transparent discussion of limitations and negative/mixed results (e.g., auxiliary loss hurting in some environments, D-REPPO slightly underperforming PQN, difficulty replicating FastTD3 wall-clock claims, inability to tune RPO/DPO above PPO), which improves credibility.

Illustrative toy experiment (6-hump camel function) helps build intuition for the variance differences between score-based and pathwise estimators, and is a nice pedagogical complement to the main algorithm.
weaknesses: The method is fundamentally an engineering combination of several previously published techniques (multi-step TD-λ, max-entropy RL, KL/relative-entropy trust regions à la REPS, HL-Gauss classification loss, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary tasks) rather than a new theoretical contribution; the paper offers little formal justification (e.g., bias/convergence analysis) for why the biased on-policy pathwise gradient estimator (Eq. 5) should remain reliable, relying instead on empirical demonstration.

No theoretical characterization of the bias introduced by the learned, continually-changing surrogate Q-function in the pathwise gradient, despite this bias being explicitly acknowledged as the central risk the paper is trying to manage; the KL/entropy scheme is a heuristic mitigation without guarantees.

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable: REPPO is tuned carefully with a dedicated hyperparameter search and run with 20 seeds, while several baselines (PPO, SAC numbers from prior papers, FastTD3 with only 5 seeds, RPO/DPO with admittedly limited tuning effort) are not matched in tuning/seed budget, which can inflate the apparent advantage of REPPO.

Wall-clock comparisons are incomplete — REPPO vs PPO is only shown in JAX, and FastTD3 (the strongest off-policy competitor) is excluded from wall-clock comparison due to implementation/framework issues, weakening the practical 'superior wall-clock time' claim made in the abstract.

The discrete-action variant (D-REPPO) underperforms PQN, and the paper attributes this to lacking explicit exploration noise, suggesting the proposed entropy/KL exploration mechanism is not a complete substitute for dedicated exploration strategies — this undercuts the generality claim.

The 'single hyperparameter set' robustness claim is weakened by the fact that discount factor γ and HL-Gauss min/max value ranges are still automatically tuned per environment via formulas, so the method is not purely hyperparameter-free across environments.

The auxiliary self-predictive loss is reported to have inconsistent (sometimes harmful) effects across environments, suggesting that practitioners must still tune per-environment architectural choices, partially undermining claims of simplicity and robustness.

Clarity could be improved: dense notation, a complex clipped/joint policy objective (Eqs. 15–16) with ad hoc switching logic, and a somewhat convoluted algorithm box make it hard to assess exactly why each design choice is necessary versus simply empirically beneficial.

Overlap with closely related recent hybrid on/off-policy work (PQN, FastTD3, MPO/V-MPO) is substantial; the incremental novelty over these methods (mainly the joint entropy-KL tuning and purely on-policy Q target) is real but modest, and the paper's positioning sometimes understates how close prior work already is.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open problem: enabling low-variance pathwise policy gradients in a fully on-policy setting without large replay buffers, which is a practically significant combination not previously demonstrated at this scale.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: 20 seeds per task across 30+ continuous-control tasks from two GPU-parallelized benchmark suites (MuJoCo Playground DMC, ManiSkill3), plus a discrete-action extension evaluated on Atari-10, using rigorous statistical reporting (bootstrapped CIs, IQM/median per Agarwal et al. methodology).

Comprehensive ablation studies isolating the contribution of each architectural/algorithmic component (HL-Gauss cross-entropy loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-predictive loss, KL regularization) at multiple data scales, clarifying which components matter most and under what conditions.

Practically relevant comparisons beyond raw return: wall-clock time, memory footprint vs. off-policy methods (FastTD3 with constrained buffer), and a 'reliable success' stability metric that captures training robustness, not just final performance.
A single hyperparameter configuration is shown to transfer robustly across dozens of tasks, which is a meaningful practical contribution for usability.
The illustrative toy experiment (Section 2.2) and Figure 2 provide clear intuition for why pathwise estimators reduce variance relative to score-based estimators.

Honest and transparent discussion of implementation/framework limitations (e.g., JAX vs PyTorch wall-clock comparison caveats, inability to replicate FastTD3's reported speed), which strengthens scientific credibility.
Good positioning relative to a large body of related work (MPO, V-MPO, PQN, FastTD3, trust-region methods), clarifying what is genuinely new versus adapted.
weaknesses: The approach lacks formal theoretical analysis of the bias introduced by using a learned, possibly inaccurate Q-function as a pathwise gradient surrogate in the on-policy regime; justification is largely empirical/heuristic rather than bounded theoretically.

Several core design choices (not recomputing TD targets across epochs, multi-epoch reuse without importance correction) are stated but not rigorously analyzed for the bias/variance tradeoffs they introduce, despite being central to the on-policy claim.
There is a broken cross-reference ('in ??') and an apparently truncated sentence about code availability, suggesting incomplete proofreading/editing before submission.

Much of the architectural machinery (HL-Gauss, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary loss) is directly adapted from prior off-policy work; the genuine novelty is concentrated in the on-policy TD-λ + joint entropy/KL tuning scheme, making the overall contribution more incremental/integrative than foundational.

Some comparisons are weakened by practical limitations acknowledged by the authors themselves (e.g., fewer seeds for FastTD3 due to inability to reproduce its reported speed, smaller GPUs used), which could affect the fairness of wall-clock/performance comparisons.

The discrete-action variant (D-REPPO) underperforms PQN with limited analysis of why, and evaluation there is less extensive (no ablations, single benchmark, high per-game variance) compared to the continuous-action results.
Normalization of returns by the best algorithm's achieved maximum (for aggregation) is a methodological choice with potential sensitivity that isn't deeply justified or stress-tested.
Missing comparisons to some other relevant modern on-policy/trust-region baselines beyond PPO, SAC, FastTD3, RPO, and DPO, which could better contextualize the claimed state-of-the-art status.
